title: Teacher-Free Self-Training Amplifies but Does Not Compound:A Pass@𝐾 Crossover on a Free-Verifier Domain

paper.title: Teacher-Free Self-Training Amplifies but Does Not Compound: A Pass@ K K Crossover on a Free-Verifier Domain
paper.abstract:
Abstract When a language model trains on its own verified outputs, does it acquire capability beyond its base, or merely get better at expressing capability
the base already had? We make the question decidable with a teacher-free
“constellation”—a generator, a learned critic, and a free exact
verifier—on a FlashFill-style “trapdoor” DSL, where verified (problem,
solution) pairs are cheap to synthesize, hard to invert, and free to check
exactly. Everything runs on one 4-bit Qwen3-4B on a single 24 GB GPU, with no
model in the loop larger than the base. We report three findings.
(i) Critic-guided selection beats verifier-filtered best-of- k k by + 9.1 +9.1 pp
( 6 / 6 6/6 seeds), with the entire gain localized to tasks where candidates disagree
on held-out inputs. (ii) Per-round STaR self-training raises the ceiling but
never accelerates—the gain tracks remaining headroom and decelerates across K = 4 K{=}4 independent training trajectories. (iii) The domain has no clean
zero-capability frontier, so the usual “ 0 % → 0\%\!\to\! climb = = emergence” test
is invalid here. A measured pass@ K K crossover settles the diagnosis: the
trained model wins at the operating budget (pass@8) but the base overtakes it at a large budget (pass@ 64 64 ) on every trajectory, so self-training concentrates probability mass rather than expanding reach. This is
amplification, not compounding. ( K = 4 K{=}4 is indicative, not yet a robust
across-trajectory CI.)

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Self-improvement loops for language models raise a question that is easy to state and surprisingly hard to answer cleanly. When a system trains on its own verified outputs, does it compound capability—following a trajectory whose per-round returns are self-reinforcing and that eventually lifts the model past the reach of its own base distribution—or does it merely amplify , sharpening and surfacing capability the base could already reach given enough sampling? Two recurring habits blur the distinction. First, most loops place a stronger teacher somewhere in the chain (a larger model, a reward model, a human), which caps any apparent novelty at the teacher’s level by construction, so one can never tell whether the loop itself produced the gain. Second, “emergence” is routinely declared whenever a metric moves off an apparent zero, even when that zero is a sampling artifact rather than a genuine inability. Our first move is to make the distinction operational rather than rhetorical. Following what has become standard practice in the elicitation-versus-acquisition literature [ 11 , 6 ] , we take the base model’s pass@ K K curve at large K K to be its reachable frontier—the set of problems it can solve if allowed enough independent attempts—and define the two outcomes against it: • amplification : per-round improvement that is monotone but non-accelerating, and whose ceiling at the operating budget stays under the base model’s large- K K envelope. The loop is surfacing reachable-but-rare programs, not new ones. • compounding : per-round gain that accelerates, or a ceiling that breaks above the base large- K K envelope—genuinely new reachability, of the kind prolonged RL is reported to produce [ 8 ] . We want to be clear about what we are and are not claiming. The level of the ceiling does rise across rounds in our experiments; self-training visibly helps. Our contribution is that the rise is headroom-paced and non-accelerating, and—by the measured pass@ K K crossover of Fig. 2 , in which the base overtakes the trained model at large K K on every training trajectory—it is amplification, not compounding. The second move is the choice of domain. We isolate the question with a “trapdoor domain” : a problem class in which forward generation of verified (problem, solution) pairs is cheap, backward solving is hard for the model, and verification is a free, total, and exact function. A single object—an exact interpreter for a small string-transformation language—then plays three roles at once. It is the verifier; it is the engine of a teacher-free data-synthesis pipeline; and, because no larger model’s judgment ever enters the loop, it is what keeps genuine novelty possible rather than capping it at a teacher’s competence. That last point is what lets a negative result here mean something: if compounding were going to appear, the construction would not have prevented it.

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: 1. A fully teacher-free generator/critic/verifier constellation on a trapdoor string-transformation DSL, runnable on a single 24 GB GPU, with every component and analysis instrument unit-tested. 2. Evidence that critic-guided selection beats verifier-filtered best-of- k k , together with a consistency check that localizes the entire gain to the structurally-relevant subset—the tasks where surviving candidates disagree on held-out inputs. 3. A three-round, two-distribution self-training trajectory that exhibits headroom-paced amplification without acceleration or collapse, supported by a confound-resistant gradient metric. The metric is headroom-normalized (so a low-base axis is not credited for climbing faster simply because it started lower), low-base-controlled (it carries a built-in control axis at comparable starting height), and same-seed paired (so per-round gain is separated from evaluation-split noise). 4. A measured pass@ K K crossover that confirms the amplification diagnosis: the trained model wins at the operating budget but the base overtakes it at large K K , robustly across four independent training trajectories on both task distributions (Fig. 2 ). 5. A negative methodological finding: in a compositional DSL, task cells that read zero at small sample counts are undersampling artifacts rather than capability frontiers, so the naive “ 0 % → 0\%\!\to\! climb = = emergence” test is invalid here. This is a direct reply to existence-of-compounding claims grounded in zero-pass@ k k cells [ 8 ] .

sections.heading: Elicitation vs. acquisition—the question we inherit.
sections.text: Whether training on verified outputs acquires capability beyond the base model or merely elicits latent capability is the central open question of the current RLVR literature, and it is precisely our amplification-versus-compounding distinction in a different regime. Yue et al. [11] make the strongest elicitation case: across model families, RL algorithms, and math/code/visual benchmarks, RL-trained models beat their base at low k k (pass@1) but are overtaken by the base at large k k , with the boundary of solvable problems narrowing as training proceeds; their coverage and perplexity analysis places the successful RL traces inside the base model’s own sampling distribution. The methodological lesson we take from them is the instrument itself—that the hypotheses are separated by pass@ k k at large k k , not by pass@1 (§ 4.4 , Fig. 2 ).

sections.heading: The counter-case.
sections.text: Liu et al. [8] (ProRL) contest the elicitation thesis on its own metric. With KL control, reference-policy resetting, and a diverse task suite, prolonged RL raises pass@ k k across the whole range and solves instances the base fails at any budget ( 0 % 0\% pass@ k k ), including out-of-training-size generalization on a graph-coloring task. This is the clearest existence proof of compounding, and it is the direct foil for two of our results: the no-zero-frontier finding (§ 6.5 ) and our out-of-training atom-count generalization on the hard bank. We do not observe the ProRL phenomenon, and we argue the difference is regime-bound—teacher-free SFT-STaR with a fixed base and no exploration bonus, a few rounds rather than thousands of steps—and possibly induced by our free exact verifier, which only ever reinforces correct-and-reachable programs and so has no way to push outward.

sections.heading: Self-training / bootstrapping.
sections.text: Our loop sits in the STaR [ 12 ] / rejection-sampling-FT [ 10 ] / ReST [ 4 ] family: keep model-generated, verifier-confirmed outputs as supervised fine-tuning targets, then retrain. What sets our instance apart is that it is teacher-free by construction—the verifier is a total exact interpreter, not a model or a reward net—so the ceiling cannot be a teacher’s competence in disguise. This matters in light of Yue et al. [11] ’s finding that distillation, unlike RL, does import a teacher’s reasoning patterns; we have removed that channel entirely.

sections.heading: Diversity collapse and our no-collapse result.
sections.text: A growing line of work formalizes why accuracy-optimizing post-training collapses generation diversity. Dang et al. [2] document pass@ k k deterioration under SFT and self-improvement, give a bias–variance decomposition of expected pass@ k k , and mitigate it via weight interpolation (WiSE-FT); differential smoothing [ 3 ] supplies a selection/reinforcement-bias account together with a reward fix; He et al. [6] trace RL’s weak multi-sample performance to an inability to reinforce low-probability correct samples; and Li et al. [7] optimize diversity and quality jointly. Against this backdrop, our observation that STaR-data diversity rises while the pass@8 ceiling does not regress is a contrasting data point—with one caveat we state plainly: our diversity metric is solution-set cardinality under a free verifier, not the entropy or n n -gram diversity these works track, so the comparison is qualitative rather than a refutation.

sections.heading: Program synthesis from examples.
sections.text: The domain is inductive programming-by-example in the FlashFill lineage [ 5 ] . Our contribution there is not a synthesizer but the use of a free exact verifier as a teacher-free reward.

sections.heading: Positioning.
sections.text: We land on the elicitation side of Yue et al. [11] , but in a regime that line has not examined: teacher-free iterated SFT on a domain with a free, total, exact verifier, where “reachable” can in principle be measured exactly via large- K K pass@ K K and the no-teacher construction removes the distillation escape hatch. The combination we report—no compounding and no collapse—is one that neither pole of the debate predicts for a single run.

sections.heading: What we baseline against.
sections.text: Each of our three claims is internally baselined against the correct published referent, so that no external benchmark is silently missing. Critic-guided selection is compared to verifier-filtered best-of- k k (“naive-pick”), which is best-of- n n selection against a verifier [ 1 ] —the standard baseline a learned selector must beat, and which our critic beats on 6 / 6 6/6 seeds. The self-training trajectory is faithful STaR [ 12 ] : verifier-only rejection sampling on the model’s own generations, retrain, repeat, with the critic confined to eval-time selection and kept out of the training loop. The method is therefore the published method, and the trajectory is itself the baseline. Finally, the amplification-versus-compounding adjudication is baselined against the base model’s own pass@ K K curve at large K K [ 11 ] , measured on a public artifact (Qwen3-4B). No external PBE accuracy number is missing: each claim is relative by construction and is compared to the standard referent for its own question.

sections.heading: 3.1 DSL and verifier
sections.text: The substrate is a small language of FlashFill-style string transforms, with the following grammar: ⬇ Expr := Concat ([ Atom , ...]) Atom := ConstStr ( s ) | SubStr ( Pos , Pos ) | Case ( op , Atom ) op in { upper , lower , cap } Pos := CPos ( k ) # absolute index , k may be negative | MatchPos ( tok , n , side ) # nth match of tok , start | end boundary tok in { WORD , DIGITS , UPPER , LOWER } The interpreter run(prog, s) is total or raises : an out-of-range position raises PosError rather than silently clamping into bounds. This is a deliberate design choice. Clamping would let two programs that agree on the visible examples but diverge elsewhere look identical, and that divergence is exactly the signal we want to preserve. Correctness is decided by exact string equality, so the verifier has zero training cost and zero learned opinion. As a sanity guarantee on the representation, a canonical text renderer and its exact inverse parser are round-trip-proven: 0 0 structural and 0 0 behavioral failures over 5000 5000 sampled programs.

sections.heading: 3.2 Trapdoor task generation
sections.text: A task is built forward, from a known program. We sample a random program, run it on random structured inputs (names, dates, emails, codes), reject degenerate outputs (empty or identity), and keep tasks that yield at least N N distinct examples. Two measured properties make the resulting tasks usable. The generator has ∼ 70 % {\sim}70\% non-degenerate yield, so producing data is cheap; and tasks are discriminative at the 0.5 % 0.5\% level—a random different program satisfies a task’s visible examples only 0.5 % 0.5\% of the time ( 5 5 spurious solves over n = 1000 n{=}1000 probes, namely 200 200 tasks × 5 \times\,5 random alternative programs each). A task therefore pins down its program tightly enough to carry real signal rather than admitting many trivial fits.

sections.heading: 3.3 Structural task classes
sections.text: For analysis only—never as a training signal—each program is bucketed by a deterministic structural signature: its atom count plus its set of flags ( sub , const , match , case , neg ), e.g. a3+sub+const+match+neg . The gradient study of § 4.4 uses four overlapping analysis axes drawn from these signatures: const-anchored , match-without-const (which we call the weak axis), neg-bearing , and case-bearing .

sections.heading: 4.1 Roles
sections.text: The system is a constellation of four roles, three of which share a single base model through swappable adapters: • Verifier — dsl.run . Total, exact, and free; it carries no parameters and no learned judgment. • Generator — a 4B LoRA adapter that maps visible examples → \to program . • Critic — a 4B LoRA adapter implementing a generative yes/no classifier, ( examples , candidate ) → generalizes? (\text{examples},\text{candidate})\to\text{generalizes?} , trained on the generator’s verifier-labeled candidates and used at inference by ranking candidates on the P ⁡ ( yes ) − P ⁡ ( no ) P(\text{yes})-P(\text{no}) logit margin. The reason a learned critic is needed at all is subtle: at selection time only the visible examples are available, so the verifier can confirm that a candidate is consistent with what is visible, but it cannot adjudicate held-out generalization until after a pick has been committed. The critic is what fills that gap. • Conductor — model-free; it holds the blackboard state and the termination rule.

sections.heading: 4.2 The loop
sections.text: A single pass through the system proceeds in five steps. (1) Split each task’s examples into a visible set and a held-out set. (2) The generator proposes k k candidate programs from the visible examples. (3) The verifier discards any candidate that fails a visible example—free and total, so this costs nothing. (4) The critic ranks the survivors and the argmax is selected. (5) The verifier adjudicates the chosen candidate on the held-out examples, which is what tells us whether the pick truly generalized.

sections.heading: 4.3 Teacher-free self-training (STaR)
sections.text: Self-training proceeds in rounds. In each round we run the current generator over fresh, non-bank tasks and keep only the model-generated, verifier-confirmed generalizing programs as new supervised fine-tuning targets, then train the next generator on them. The secret program behind a task is used only to label the task by structural axis; it is never emitted as a target (a property checked by smoke_roundlogic ). This is precisely what makes any gain self-bootstrapped rather than quietly distilled from an oracle. We deliberately run pure per-round STaR—each generator is trained on that round’s data alone, with no cumulative anchor to earlier rounds—both to make any collapse maximally visible and to hold the method fixed across the trajectory.

sections.heading: 4.4 Confound-resistant gradient metric
sections.text: To ask whether self-training improved the weak axis preferentially , we cannot simply compare raw percentage-point gains: an axis that starts lower will climb more in raw points at equal effort, so a raw comparison is confounded by starting height. We instead report the fraction of available ceiling headroom closed per axis, headroom-closed = Δ rate 1 − rate 0 , \text{headroom-closed}\;=\;\frac{\Delta_{\text{rate}}}{1-\text{rate}_{0}}, which normalizes each axis by how much room it had to improve. To guard against the residual worry that any low-base axis improves more, the neg-bearing axis serves as a built-in low-base control : only if the weak axis closes more headroom than both the easy axis and the comparably-low-base neg control can the effect be attributed to weakness rather than to generic low-base regression. Separately, the base model’s large- K K pass@ K K envelope—measured on its own—is what ultimately adjudicates amplification versus compounding: the trained model’s ceiling stays under it (Fig. 2 , § 8 ).

sections.heading: 5 Experimental setup
sections.text: • Base model: Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 [ 9 ] , 4-bit nf4 quantization, bf16 compute. • Adapters: LoRA r = 16 r{=}16 , α = 32 \alpha{=}32 , dropout 0.05 0.05 , all-linear targets ( ∼ 0.81 % {\sim}0.81\% trainable parameters); QLoRA with paged_adamw_8bit . • Hardware: a single RTX 3090 (24 GB). The generator and critic adapters run as two sequential passes over one quantized base, with the generator freed between passes—the two adapters cannot co-reside in full precision at this budget. • Frozen eval banks (never trained on, sha-pinned, with tamper-evident metadata): easy ( max_atoms=3 , 200 200 tasks, sha 512ddf40… ); hard ( max_atoms=4 , 200 200 tasks, sha 49807fcc… , an out-of-training atom count). Each task carries a 12 12 -example pool, with the visible/held-out split carved at eval time. • Default regime: visible = 2 =2 , 8 8 generator samples per task—the divergence-maximizing peak of the Stage-0 sweep (§ 6.1 ). • Software (probe-confirmed at run time): torch 2.12+cu130, transformers 5.9, trl 1.5.1, peft 0.19.1, bitsandbytes 0.49.2, Python 3.13.

sections.heading: No collapse.
sections.text: Self-training did not degrade the sampler. The STaR-data diversity_mean (distinct generalizing programs per solved task) rose from 2.79 2.79 to 4.05 4.05 ; the any-visible-consistent rate rose on both banks (paired + 3.8 % / + 2.3 % +3.8\%/+2.3\% on easy, + 2.2 % / + 4.6 % +2.2\%/+4.6\% on hard); and the statistically-solid easy class a1+const ( n = 34 n{=}34 ) never regressed. Where the gains shrink—on the easy bank—it is exhaustion of reachable headroom under a fixed base, not degeneration of the sampler.

sections.heading: 6.5 No clean zero-capability frontier exists in this DSL
sections.text: A natural worry about any emergence claim is whether the apparent zeros are real. Here they are not. Trained only on max_atoms ≤ 3 {\leq}3 , gen_v0 already solves unseen 4-atom classes on the hard bank at 25 25 – 50 % 50\% ceiling (for example a4+sub+const+match+case at 50 % 50\% and a4+sub+const+match+neg at 44 % 44\% )—comparable to the same token-sets at atom- 3 3 . The Concat structure is compositional enough that “one more atom” is simply not out-of-distribution. The only cells that read zero are small- n n ( 0 / 3 0/3 – 0 / 5 0/5 ), and they are undersampling artifacts : the same classes solve at 5 5 – 38 % 38\% once measured at population scale. Declaring emergence because such a cell climbs off zero would be mistaking variance for capability—which is exactly why we rely on the relative-gradient test of § 4.4 rather than a naive zero-floor test. This speaks directly to existence-of-compounding claims that rest on zero-pass@ k k cells [ 8 ] : in a compositional domain, such cells must first be shown non-trivial at population scale.

sections.heading: The real wall is above the ceiling, not at zero.
sections.text: The genuine bound on this paradigm is not a zero-frontier but a gap higher up. At K = 64 K{=}64 the base produces a visible-consistent (possibly overfit) program for 79.0 % 79.0\% (easy) / 68.5 % 68.5\% (hard) of tasks, yet only 68.0 % 68.0\% / 57.5 % 57.5\% ever yield a generalizing one—a stable ∼ 11 {\sim}11 pp ( 22 22 -task) gap on both banks, a band in which the base reliably finds a fitting-but-wrong program and never the correct one. That gap, not a zero-frontier, is the real generator-capacity bound: the region no amount of selection or self-training over a fixed base can enter, and hence the ceiling on what this paradigm can deliver. Figure 2: The measurement that adjudicates the headline, now populated. Solid markers are measured pass@8 ceilings of v 0 / v 1 / v 2 v_{0}/v_{1}/v_{2} (seed 1234) on the easy (circles) and hard (squares) banks; dashed lines are the base v 0 v_{0} pass@ 64 64 ceiling per bank—a lower bound on the reachable frontier. On both banks the rising pass@8 trajectory stays under the base pass@ 64 64 line (easy 53.0 % 53.0\% vs 68.0 % 68.0\% ; hard 46.0 % 46.0\% vs 57.5 % 57.5\% ): self-training surfaces reachable-but-rare programs without breaking above base reach—amplification, not compounding. Because pass@ 64 64 lower-bounds K → ∞ K\!\to\!\infty , the gap is conservative.

sections.heading: Amplification, not (observed) compounding.
sections.text: Every positive movement we saw traces back to surfacing reachable-but-rare capability—the selector recovering headroom, and STaR enriching the sampling tail. Nothing ever climbed off a population-scale zero. It is worth emphasizing that the teacher-free construction kept genuine novelty possible ; the finding, over three rounds, is simply that it did not appear . The crossover is the full Yue et al. [11] signature, now measured on both sides (pass@ K K at seed 1234): v 2 v_{2} beats the base at the operating budget (pass@8 53.0 % / 46.0 % 53.0\%/46.0\% vs base 46.0 % / 38.0 % 46.0\%/38.0\% , easy/hard) but the base overtakes v 2 v_{2} at a large budget (pass@64 base 68.0 % / 57.5 % 68.0\%/57.5\% vs v 2 v_{2} 61.5 % / 52.5 % 61.5\%/52.5\% ). The overtaking is train-seed robust—it holds for all four independent training trajectories on both banks ( 4 / 4 4/4 ; § 8 ). We therefore confirm the large- K K coverage narrowing rather than escaping it: self-training concentrates probability mass, making rare-but-reachable solutions common (so it wins at k = 8 k{=}8 ) while lowering large- K K coverage (so it loses at k = 64 k{=}64 ). The within-model K K -scaling makes the concentration concrete: raising the sample budget from 8 8 to 64 64 adds + 22 +22 pp of ceiling for the base ( 46 → 68 46\to 68 on easy) but only + 8.5 +8.5 pp for v 2 v_{2} ( 53 → 61.5 53\to 61.5 ). The trained model extracts less than half the marginal coverage per extra sample—the signature of mass piled onto fewer modal solutions per task. This is predicted by , not merely consistent with, the collapse literature: SFT on accuracy-selected targets concentrates probability on the modal solution even when the harvested targets are diverse [ 2 , 3 ] . The rising diversity_mean is therefore not in tension with the narrowing, because the two measure different things: diversity_mean is the cardinality of the STaR-harvest solution set during data generation, whereas the narrowing is in the eval-time pass@ K K coverage of the trained model. Harvest diversity rises while the trained model’s sampling coverage narrows—exactly the dissociation those accounts imply.

sections.heading: Why headroom-paced, not collapse.
sections.text: The per-round ceiling gain scales with how much headroom remains: it shrinks on the near-ceiling easy bank ( + 6.4 → + 2.3 +6.4\to+2.3 ) but holds on the low-base hard bank ( + 3.2 → + 3.9 +3.2\to+3.9 ), and diversity rises throughout. Where the gains shrink, it is exhaustion of the reachable frontier under a fixed base, not degeneration of the sampler. A frontier the base cannot reach is, by construction, invisible to a loop that can only train on what the verifier confirms—which is also why our setting, unlike prolonged RL with an exploration bonus [ 8 ] , has no mechanism to manufacture compounding even in principle.

sections.heading: Selector value erodes as the generator sharpens.
sections.text: Divergence—the critic’s only workspace—fell across the trajectory, the same dynamic reached from a different direction at the visible-rich end of the Stage-0 sweep. There is a practical lesson here for anyone designing such constellations: improving one role can shrink another role’s niche, so the value of a learned selector is not static across a self-training run.

sections.heading: What is and is not novel here.
sections.text: We want to be candid about what is surprising. The crossover direction is the expected one: under Yue et al. [11] , teacher-free training (no distillation) is predicted to stay base-bounded, because distillation is their only capability-importing intervention—so we do not claim the direction as a discovery. The contribution is threefold: (i) confirming the effect in a regime that line has not examined—teacher-free iterated SFT with a free, total, exact verifier, where “reachable” is measured exactly via large- K K pass@ K K ; (ii) the dissociation between rising harvest diversity and narrowing model coverage; and (iii) the no-zero-frontier methodology, which shows that existence-of-compounding claims resting on zero-pass@ k k cells must first establish those cells non-trivial at population scale.

sections.heading: Scope.
sections.text: One causal caveat deserves emphasis. The free, total, exact verifier is doing heavy lifting: it reinforces only correct-and-reachable programs and never explores, so “no compounding” may be a property of this verification regime rather than of self-training in general. A noisy verifier, a learned reward model, or a teacher could behave differently. The result is, in that sense, domain-internal (§ 8 ).

sections.heading: 8 Limitations (honesty bounds)
sections.text: • Statistical power. The gen_v0 baseline, the Stage-1 loop, and the full v 0 / v 1 / v 2 v_{0}/v_{1}/v_{2} ceiling trajectory are six-seed CI’d on both banks (eval-split variance of fixed adapters). The no-acceleration claim additionally survives train-seed variance: K = 4 K{=}4 independent training trajectories decelerate on both banks (§ 6.4 , Tier 3). The power limits that remain are honest ones: K = 4 K{=}4 is small (the across-trajectory stdev is indicative, not a robust CI— ≥ 5 \geq 5 would be wanted), the train-seed replication covers the no-acceleration claim but not every per-round magnitude, and the weak-axis gradient (App. C ) is still single-seed-per-bank. A ≥ 5 \geq 5 -seed train-seed CI for a robust across-trajectory interval is left to future work. • The decisive pass@ K K measurement: the full crossover, at K = 64 K{=}64 , train-seed robust. We measure both halves of the Yue et al. [11] signature at a matched K = 64 K{=}64 : v 2 v_{2} wins at the operating budget (pass@8 53.0 % / 46.0 % 53.0\%/46.0\% vs base 46.0 % / 38.0 % 46.0\%/38.0\% ) and the base overtakes v 2 v_{2} at the large budget (pass@64 base 68.0 % / 57.5 % 68.0\%/57.5\% vs v 2 v_{2} 61.5 % / 52.5 % 61.5\%/52.5\% ), on both banks. The overtaking holds across all four independent training trajectories: every v 2 v_{2} pass@64 ceiling stays below the base’s on both banks ( 4 / 4 4/4 ; easy margins 6 6 – 13 13 tasks, hard 7 7 – 15 15 ; results/crossover_tier3.json ), so the level test is train-seed robust and not a single-trajectory artifact. Two residual caveats: pass@ 64 64 lower-bounds K → ∞ K\!\to\!\infty (the true overtaking margin is at least this large), and the pass@ 64 64 ceilings are single eval-seed—though the + 15.0 +15.0 / + 11.5 +11.5 pp v 2 v_{2} @8-to-base@64 gaps dwarf the ∼ 2 {\sim}2 pp eval-split noise, so eval-seed is not a fragile dependence. Per-point error bars (6-seed base and v 2 v_{2} pass@ 64 64 CIs) are left to future work. • n = 1 n=1 on most axes of generality: one base model, one GPU, one DSL, one program prior. The results are domain-internal and support no external “FlashFill capability” claim. • Shared-base adapter attribution. The generator and critic are LoRA adapters over the same frozen base, so they are not independent; a separately-based critic would be a cleaner test, and we have not done it. • Only two STaR rounds. The no-acceleration claim (that per-round gain does not increase) rests on two paired steps, and the still-climbing hard bank could behave differently with more rounds. The crossover level claim (that the trained model stays below the base at large K K ) is, by contrast, round-count-robust: it would survive additional rounds unless some later v N v_{N} broke above the base envelope—which would itself be the compounding signal we are looking for. • No cross-domain benchmark. All comparisons are internal-relative (critic vs. best-of- k k , trained vs. base pass@ K K , both on our DSL). The baselines are instances of published methods (best-of- n n /self-consistency, STaR, base pass@ K K ) and are the correct referents for the questions asked (§ 2 ), but we do not report accuracy on a standard PBE benchmark such as SyGuS, so the result is domain-internal.

sections.heading: 9 Reproducibility
sections.text: The evaluation banks are frozen and sha-pinned with tamper-evident metadata sidecars (easy 512ddf40… , hard 49807fcc… ), and regeneration refuses to overwrite them without an explicit flag. Every RNG seed is recorded in each artifact’s metadata, and the STaR data carries a mandatory frozen-bank leakage-exclusion guard that surfaces its reject counts. All analysis instruments are pure-stdlib and unit-tested—every instrument and the stdlib core carries a unit smoke test, all green—and the multi-seed aggregator prints every per-seed raw count and refuses to average over inconsistent task denominators. The stdlib core has zero third-party dependencies; the GPU stack is pinned behind a committed-lockfile uv extra. The code and all result artifacts are released at https://github.com/izzortsi/trapdoor-loom under the CC0 1.0 public-domain dedication. The public repository de-anonymizes the authors, so this preprint is non-blind by design.

August 24, 2026 Abstract When a language model trains on its own verified outputs, does it acquire capability beyond its base, or merely get better at expressing capability the base already had? We make the question decidable with a teacher-free “constellation”—a generator, a learned critic, and a free exact verifier—on a FlashFill-style “trapdoor” DSL, where verified (problem, solution) pairs are cheap to synthesize, hard to invert, and free to check exactly. Everything runs on one 4-bit Qwen3-4B on a single 24 GB GPU, with no model in the loop larger than the base. We report three findings. (i) Critic-guided selection beats verifier-filtered best-of- k k by + 9.1 +9.1 pp ( 6 / 6 6/6 seeds), with the entire gain localized to tasks where candidates disagree on held-out inputs. (ii) Per-round STaR self-training raises the ceiling but never accelerates—the gain tracks remaining headroom and decelerates across K = 4 K{=}4 independent training trajectories. (iii) The domain has no clean zero-capability frontier, so the usual “ 0 % → 0\%\!\to\! climb = = emergence” test is invalid here. A measured pass@ K K crossover settles the diagnosis: the trained model wins at the operating budget (pass@8) but the base overtakes it at a large budget (pass@ 64 64 ) on every trajectory, so self-training concentrates probability mass rather than expanding reach. This is amplification, not compounding. ( K = 4 K{=}4 is indicative, not yet a robust across-trajectory CI.) 1 Introduction Self-improvement loops for language models raise a question that is easy to state and surprisingly hard to answer cleanly. When a system trains on its own verified outputs, does it compound capability—following a trajectory whose per-round returns are self-reinforcing and that eventually lifts the model past the reach of its own base distribution—or does it merely amplify , sharpening and surfacing capability the base could already reach given enough sampling? Two recurring habits blur the distinction. First, most loops place a stronger teacher somewhere in the chain (a larger model, a reward model, a human), which caps any apparent novelty at the teacher’s level by construction, so one can never tell whether the loop itself produced the gain. Second, “emergence” is routinely declared whenever a metric moves off an apparent zero, even when that zero is a sampling artifact rather than a genuine inability. Our first move is to make the distinction operational rather than rhetorical. Following what has become standard practice in the elicitation-versus-acquisition literature [ 11 , 6 ] , we take the base model’s pass@ K K curve at large K K to be its reachable frontier—the set of problems it can solve if allowed enough independent attempts—and define the two outcomes against it: • amplification : per-round improvement that is monotone but non-accelerating, and whose ceiling at the operating budget stays under the base model’s large- K K envelope. The loop is surfacing reachable-but-rare programs, not new ones. • compounding : per-round gain that accelerates, or a ceiling that breaks above the base large- K K envelope—genuinely new reachability, of the kind prolonged RL is reported to produce [ 8 ] . We want to be clear about what we are and are not claiming. The level of the ceiling does rise across rounds in our experiments; self-training visibly helps. Our contribution is that the rise is headroom-paced and non-accelerating, and—by the measured pass@ K K crossover of Fig. 2 , in which the base overtakes the trained model at large K K on every training trajectory—it is amplification, not compounding. The second move is the choice of domain. We isolate the question with a “trapdoor domain” : a problem class in which forward generation of verified (problem, solution) pairs is cheap, backward solving is hard for the model, and verification is a free, total, and exact function. A single object—an exact interpreter for a small string-transformation language—then plays three roles at once. It is the verifier; it is the engine of a teacher-free data-synthesis pipeline; and, because no larger model’s judgment ever enters the loop, it is what keeps genuine novelty possible rather than capping it at a teacher’s competence. That last point is what lets a negative result here mean something: if compounding were going to appear, the construction would not have prevented it. Contributions. 1. A fully teacher-free generator/critic/verifier constellation on a trapdoor string-transformation DSL, runnable on a single 24 GB GPU, with every component and analysis instrument unit-tested. 2. Evidence that critic-guided selection beats verifier-filtered best-of- k k , together with a consistency check that localizes the entire gain to the structurally-relevant subset—the tasks where surviving candidates disagree on held-out inputs. 3. A three-round, two-distribution self-training trajectory that exhibits headroom-paced amplification without acceleration or collapse, supported by a confound-resistant gradient metric. The metric is headroom-normalized (so a low-base axis is not credited for climbing faster simply because it started lower), low-base-controlled (it carries a built-in control axis at comparable starting height), and same-seed paired (so per-round gain is separated from evaluation-split noise). 4. This is a direct reply to existence-of-compounding claims grounded in zero-pass@ k k cells [ 8 ] . 2 Related work Elicitation vs. acquisition—the question we inherit. Whether training on verified outputs acquires capability beyond the base model or merely elicits latent capability is the central open question of the current RLVR literature, and it is precisely our amplification-versus-compounding distinction in a different regime. Yue et al. [11] make the strongest elicitation case: across model families, RL algorithms, and math/code/visual benchmarks, RL-trained models beat their base at low k k (pass@1) but are overtaken by the base at large k k , with the boundary of solvable problems narrowing as training proceeds; their coverage and perplexity analysis places the successful RL traces inside the base model’s own sampling distribution. The methodological lesson we take from them is the instrument itself—that the hypotheses are separated by pass@ k k at large k k , not by pass@1 (§ 4.4 , Fig. 2 ). The counter-case. Liu et al. [8] (ProRL) contest the elicitation thesis on its own metric. With KL control, reference-policy resetting, and a diverse task suite, prolonged RL raises pass@ k k across the whole range and solves instances the base fails at any budget ( 0 % 0\% pass@ k k ), including out-of-training-size generalization on a graph-coloring task. This is the clearest existence proof of compounding, and it is the direct foil for two of our results: the no-zero-frontier finding (§ 6.5 ) and our out-of-training atom-count generalization on the hard bank. We do not observe the ProRL phenomenon, and we argue the difference is regime-bound—teacher-free SFT-STaR with a fixed base and no exploration bonus, a few rounds rather than thousands of steps—and possibly induced by our free exact verifier, which only ever reinforces correct-and-reachable programs and so has no way to push outward. Self-training / bootstrapping. Our loop sits in the STaR [ 12 ] / rejection-sampling-FT [ 10 ] / ReST [ 4 ] family: keep model-generated, verifier-confirmed outputs as supervised fine-tuning targets, then retrain. What sets our instance apart is that it is teacher-free by construction—the verifier is a total exact interpreter, not a model or a reward net—so the ceiling cannot be a teacher’s competence in disguise. This matters in light of Yue et al. [11] ’s finding that distillation, unlike RL, does import a teacher’s reasoning patterns; we have removed that channel entirely. Diversity collapse and our no-collapse result. A growing line of work formalizes why accuracy-optimizing post-training collapses generation diversity. Dang et al. [2] document pass@ k k deterioration under SFT and self-improvement, give a bias–variance decomposition of expected pass@ k k , and mitigate it via weight interpolation (WiSE-FT); differential smoothing [ 3 ] supplies a selection/reinforcement-bias account together with a reward fix; He et al. [6] trace RL’s weak multi-sample performance to an inability to reinforce low-probability correct samples; and Li et al. [7] optimize diversity and quality jointly. Against this backdrop, our observation that STaR-data diversity rises while the pass@8 ceiling does not regress is a contrasting data point—with one caveat we state plainly: our diversity metric is solution-set cardinality under a free verifier, not the entropy or n n -gram diversity these works track, so the comparison is qualitative rather than a refutation. Program synthesis from examples. The domain is inductive programming-by-example in the FlashFill lineage [ 5 ] . Our contribution there is not a synthesizer but the use of a free exact verifier as a teacher-free reward. Positioning. We land on the elicitation side of Yue et al. The combination we report—no compounding and no collapse—is one that neither pole of the debate predicts for a single run. What we baseline against. Each of our three claims is internally baselined against the correct published referent, so that no external benchmark is silently missing. Critic-guided selection is compared to verifier-filtered best-of- k k (“naive-pick”), which is best-of- n n selection against a verifier [ 1 ] —the standard baseline a learned selector must beat, and which our critic beats on 6 / 6 6/6 seeds. This is a deliberate design choice. Clamping would let two programs that agree on the visible examples but diverge elsewhere look identical, and that divergence is exactly the signal we want to preserve. Correctness is decided by exact string equality, so the verifier has zero training cost and zero learned opinion. As a sanity guarantee on the representation, a canonical text renderer and its exact inverse parser are round-trip-proven: 0 0 structural and 0 0 behavioral failures over 5000 5000 sampled programs. 3.2 Trapdoor task generation A task is built forward, from a known program. We sample a random program, run it on random structured inputs (names, dates, emails, codes), reject degenerate outputs (empty or identity), and keep tasks that yield at least N N distinct examples. Two measured properties make the resulting tasks usable. The generator has ∼ 70 % {\sim}70\% non-degenerate yield, so producing data is cheap; and tasks are discriminative at the 0.5 % 0.5\% level—a random different program satisfies a task’s visible examples only 0.5 % 0.5\% of the time ( 5 5 spurious solves over n = 1000 n{=}1000 probes, namely 200 200 tasks × 5 \times\,5 random alternative programs each). A task therefore pins down its program tightly enough to carry real signal rather than admitting many trivial fits. 3.3 Structural task classes For analysis only—never as a training signal—each program is bucketed by a deterministic structural signature: its atom count plus its set of flags ( sub , const , match , case , neg ), e.g. a3+sub+const+match+neg . The gradient study of § 4.4 uses four overlapping analysis axes drawn from these signatures: const-anchored , match-without-const (which we call the weak axis), neg-bearing , and case-bearing . 4 Method 4.1 Roles The system is a constellation of four roles, three of which share a single base model through swappable adapters: • Verifier — dsl.run . Total, exact, and free; it carries no parameters and no learned judgment. • Generator — a 4B LoRA adapter that maps visible examples → \to program . • Critic — a 4B LoRA adapter implementing a generative yes/no classifier, ( examples , candidate ) → generalizes? (\text{examples},\text{candidate})\to\text{generalizes?} , trained on the generator’s verifier-labeled candidates and used at inference by ranking candidates on the P ⁡ ( yes ) − P ⁡ ( no ) P(\text{yes})-P(\text{no}) logit margin. The reason a learned critic is needed at all is subtle: at selection time only the visible examples are available, so the verifier can confirm that a candidate is consistent with what is visible, but it cannot adjudicate held-out generalization until after a pick has been committed. The critic is what fills that gap. • Conductor — model-free; it holds the blackboard state and the termination rule. 4.2 The loop A single pass through the system proceeds in five steps. (1) Split each task’s examples into a visible set and a held-out set. (2) The generator proposes k k candidate programs from the visible examples. (3) The verifier discards any candidate that fails a visible example—free and total, so this costs nothing. (4) The critic ranks the survivors and the argmax is selected. (5) The verifier adjudicates the chosen candidate on the held-out examples, which is what tells us whether the pick truly generalized. 4.3 Teacher-free self-training (STaR) Self-training proceeds in rounds. In each round we run the current generator over fresh, non-bank tasks and keep only the model-generated, verifier-confirmed generalizing programs as new supervised fine-tuning targets, then train the next generator on them. The secret program behind a task is used only to label the task by structural axis; it is never emitted as a target (a property checked by smoke_roundlogic ). This is precisely what makes any gain self-bootstrapped rather than quietly distilled from an oracle. We deliberately run pure per-round STaR—each generator is trained on that round’s data alone, with no cumulative anchor to earlier rounds—both to make any collapse maximally visible and to hold the method fixed across the trajectory. 4.4 Confound-resistant gradient metric To ask whether self-training improved the weak axis preferentially , we cannot simply compare raw percentage-point gains: an axis that starts lower will climb more in raw points at equal effort, so a raw comparison is confounded by starting height. We instead report the fraction of available ceiling headroom closed per axis, headroom-closed = Δ rate 1 − rate 0 , \text{headroom-closed}\;=\;\frac{\Delta_{\text{rate}}}{1-\text{rate}_{0}}, which normalizes each axis by how much room it had to improve. To guard against the residual worry that any low-base axis improves more, the neg-bearing axis serves as a built-in low-base control : only if the weak axis closes more headroom than both the easy axis and the comparably-low-base neg control can the effect be attributed to weakness rather than to generic low-base regression. Every positive movement we saw traces back to surfacing reachable-but-rare capability—the selector recovering headroom, and STaR enriching the sampling tail. Nothing ever climbed off a population-scale zero. It is worth emphasizing that the teacher-free construction kept genuine novelty possible ; the finding, over three rounds, is simply that it did not appear . The crossover is the full Yue et al. [11] signature, now measured on both sides (pass@ K K at seed 1234): v 2 v_{2} beats the base at the operating budget (pass@8 53.0 % / 46.0 % 53.0\%/46.0\% vs base 46.0 % / 38.0 % 46.0\%/38.0\% , easy/hard) but the base overtakes v 2 v_{2} at a large budget (pass@64 base 68.0 % / 57.5 % 68.0\%/57.5\% vs v 2 v_{2} 61.5 % / 52.5 % 61.5\%/52.5\% ). The overtaking is train-seed robust—it holds for all four independent training trajectories on both banks ( 4 / 4 4/4 ; § 8 ). We therefore confirm the large- K K coverage narrowing rather than escaping it: self-training concentrates probability mass, making rare-but-reachable solutions common (so it wins at k = 8 k{=}8 ) while lowering large- K K coverage (so it loses at k = 64 k{=}64 ). The within-model K K -scaling makes the concentration concrete: raising the sample budget from 8 8 to 64 64 adds + 22 +22 pp of ceiling for the base ( 46 → 68 46\to 68 on easy) but only + 8.5 +8.5 pp for v 2 v_{2} ( 53 → 61.5 53\to 61.5 ). The trained model extracts less than half the marginal coverage per extra sample—the signature of mass piled onto fewer modal solutions per task. This is predicted by , not merely consistent with, the collapse literature: SFT on accuracy-selected targets concentrates probability on the modal solution even when the harvested targets are diverse [ 2 , 3 ] . The rising diversity_mean is therefore not in tension with the narrowing, because the two measure different things: diversity_mean is the cardinality of the STaR-harvest solution set during data generation, whereas the narrowing is in the eval-time pass@ K K coverage of the trained model. Harvest diversity rises while the trained model’s sampling coverage narrows—exactly the dissociation those accounts imply. Why headroom-paced, not collapse. The per-round ceiling gain scales with how much headroom remains: it shrinks on the near-ceiling easy bank ( + 6.4 → + 2.3 +6.4\to+2.3 ) but holds on the low-base hard bank ( + 3.2 → + 3.9 +3.2\to+3.9 ), and diversity rises throughout. Where the gains shrink, it is exhaustion of the reachable frontier under a fixed base, not degeneration of the sampler. A frontier the base cannot reach is, by construction, invisible to a loop that can only train on what the verifier confirms—which is also why our setting, unlike prolonged RL with an exploration bonus [ 8 ] , has no mechanism to manufacture compounding even in principle. Selector value erodes as the generator sharpens. Divergence—the critic’s only workspace—fell across the trajectory, the same dynamic reached from a different direction at the visible-rich end of the Stage-0 sweep. There is a practical lesson here for anyone designing such constellations: improving one role can shrink another role’s niche, so the value of a learned selector is not static across a self-training run. What is and is not novel here. We want to be candid about what is surprising. The crossover direction is the expected one: under Yue et al. [11] , teacher-free training (no distillation) is predicted to stay base-bounded, because distillation is their only capability-importing intervention—so we do not claim the direction as a discovery. The contribution is threefold: (i) confirming the effect in a regime that line has not examined—teacher-free iterated SFT with a free, total, exact verifier, where “reachable” is measured exactly via large- K K pass@ K K ; (ii) the dissociation between rising harvest diversity and narrowing model coverage; and (iii) the no-zero-frontier methodology, which shows that existence-of-compounding claims resting on zero-pass@ k k cells must first establish those cells non-trivial at population scale. Scope. One causal caveat deserves emphasis. The free, total, exact verifier is doing heavy lifting: it reinforces only correct-and-reachable programs and never explores, so “no compounding” may be a property of this verification regime rather than of self-training in general. A noisy verifier, a learned reward model, or a teacher could behave differently. The result is, in that sense, domain-internal (§ 8 ). 8 Limitations (honesty bounds) • Statistical power.
